An old classic game based on one of the most iconic shows of all time. Voice performances by all the principal actors, most of whom aren't with us anymore, make this game a sentimental treasure. The missions feel like episodes of the original show. Multiple possible solutions to the game's puzzles, with both good and bad outcomes, make for a lot more replay value than you would expect from the old point-and-click genre. Find a way to score 100% on all missions, or do a blooper run to finish a campaign with the lowest possible score. And if all that isn't enough, the game makes use of a three-dimensional space combat system that still holds up well today. The battles are often criticized for being too difficult, and the DOS era graphics are very dated, but this game is high-quality entertainment for fans and non-fans alike.

This game is the definitive Star Trek TOS experience! The original cast do a respectable job reprising their roles once more as the crew of the original Enterprise. (DeForest Kelley does the best job, in my opinion) The game features both 1st person space combat and 3rd person point and click away missions. There are also regular branches in dialogue where you move the conversation along by choosing Kirk's statements/responses. Some dialogue options can have lethal consequences, so conducting yourself like a Starfleet captain yields the best results. (Yes, red shirts can die as a result of Kirk's negligence or incompetence.) This gives the game the replay value to justify many playthroughs to find all the branches in dialogue, and the events triggered by them.

The game is meant to represent the fourth season of the original series. The stories for each mission are deep and VERY well written! The final mission serves as an intense finale to the game, with a grim scene onboard a husk Starfleet vessel, scattered with the corpses of it's crew.

The production team deserves props for their creativity and immersive style. My only gripe is that second to last mission. Anybody who claims they solved that mission (specifically the door codes) without looking up the answer is full of it. Other than that, this game is a brilliant piece of Star Trek history for any gamer.

After an evening to think on my original positive review of this game, I've decided I'm changing this to a do not recommend. In my first review, immediately after playing the game (which I will leave at the bottom of this review) I'm against the idea of giving this game a thumbs down, mostly because I love Star Trek, and I don't want to poop on an old DOS game I couldn't fix an end-game glitch on. But, even ignoring that, this game is not really all that good.

Firstly, the game is broken into 7 individual "episodes", and they're all super short. The story here is next to non-existent in each, which is a real shame, because writing engaging stories is where Star Trek can really shine, and there's some idea nuggets here for stories. One is about an ancient nuclear missile base rearming itself, and the insanity that is world-ending weapons. Another is about Harry Mudd on a super science ship, selling miraculous technologies he doesn't understand as his usual snake oils. Even another is about a member planet in the Federation attempting an insurrection against the Federation! These are stories that could have some real meat to their bones, but not one of them goes anywhere. They're all interesting ideas, just sorta tacked onto the beginning of each episode with a mission given by Starfleet, maybe given a line or two during the episode, and then referenced again in the end-of-episode chatter between our three main boys, where they act like we had a profound discussion, but we... didn't. This wouldn't bug me so much, if the writers here didn't clearly show that they could do good Trek writing! 

There is good writing in here! Shock of shocks, in this boring mission writing, there's some real gold in here, it's just hidden in the use of the look and speak options, between Kirk, Spock, and McCoy during the missions! There's some genuinely great lines, usually a real nugget of gold every screen, you just need to stop, on every screen, and spend 5 minutes asking everybody in your away team a question, and looking at them. You'll get great atmospheric lines of our main trio bantering about everything from what they'd like to do to Harry Mudd, to the great tragedy of human deaths in space, but it's a bunch of effort on describing how McCoy is anxious about how many dead men he'll see on this mission, and no effort on, y'know, telling an interesting story for the episode, or even setting up who the villain of a piece is! I've heard the next game, Judgment Rites, has more dialogue, which leaves me hopeful that it might be better balanced between story writing, and general atmospheric writing you have to dig for.

In balance to these little tidbits of gold between the three amigos of the bridge of NCC 1701, no bloody A, B, C, or D, is the voice acting, specifically, from one actor. This game utilizes the voice talents of the original actors for most of the main crew, and most of them give some solid performances. McCoy is passionate and excited, Spock is thoughtful and supportive, and Kirk... Sounds like he's reading his lines as monotonously as possible. For the great overactor Shatner is, Kirk here sounds bored half the time, and unfortunately, he's the one who has the most lines. Everyone else is giving gusto to their performances, and Kirk really sounds like he's bored in a stuffy sound booth, recording lines without any since of context or meaning, which really brings the whole thing down.

There are a few other highlights, but they can't lift this game from what's a really kinda boring and short experience. The space combat gives some real sense of three dimensional ship fighting, and that's surprising as a modern gamer to see from something that run on DOS. It's no Elite Dangerous or anything, but it's a surprisingly satisfactory space ship fighting simulator, when you get some space ship fights. The intro to the game is a beautiful recreation of the TOS theme as well, given what level of audio fidelity they have. The game is also usually pretty good about not throwing any absurd point-and-click adventure puzzles at you, unless Spock out-right tells you what the weird solution is.

But none of it is enough to cover for what feels less like a Star Trek game, and more like a game that someone wrapped Star Trek around, and it doesn't feel like it delivers on being a continuation of the 5 year mission. Sorry, Star Trek, I can't recommend you to someone else, even without the game breaking glitch I had encountered at the end of the game, leaving me unable to finish you.

Star Trek 25th Anniversary is a space combat, point & click adventure RPG developed and published by Interplay Entertainment in 1992 that would help path the way for Interplay's roster of incredible RPGs. It acts as a continuation of TOS 5 year mission and all of the actor reprise their roles lending their voices making it feel like a true Star Trek production. The gameplay especially ship combat can be very challenging with a large and difficult to pick up  control system making it tedious at times. There is also a simplistic dialogue system that give the player a choice of several responses which is a nice touch. The ground adventure segments take up the larger part of the game and allow for the player to chose different approaches to a situation resulting in different outcomes. the combat is few and far between and is very easy. The player will often have to consult the game manual to find the star map and instructions to find out what to do next. there are also puzzles throughout the game which can be very challenging because of the varied amounts of interactive options and combinations.  players are scored at the end of each mission on how they handle situations and solve problems. 

If you are looking for a casual adventure game this undoubtedly is not the game for you. At £6.99  $9.66 €8.03 it is a game that can be very challenging  and unforgiving yet rewarding at times. I would however say that if you are a Trekie especially a TOS Trekkie then this is a game you should have in your collection because as previously stated it is a continuation of TOS 5 year journey voiced by the original cast with some really good writing in it that every Trekkie should at least try once. If the price seems a bit too high you can always add it to your wish list and wait for a sale. Interplay aren't exactly coming back to life anytime soon to jack up the price.

[h1]Space: the final frontier.
These are the voyages of the starship Enterprise...
[i]~Samuel A. Peeples[/i][/h1]

Ah, the [b]Star Trek[/b]... My most favorite Sci-Fi show ever and simply the most influential one out there. And not only because it captured that certain feeling that every kid has while dreaming about space, but also because of its social importance. Seriously, the show was always ahead of its time. For example, [b]Whoopi Goldberg[/b] (who'll end up playing [b]Guinan[/b] in [b]Star Trek: The Next Generation[/b]) still remembers her shock from seeing the black lady on TV. Who wasn't playing maid. [b]Star Trek[/b] is deep, guys... [b]Star Trek[/b] is deep. Unfortunately, we never had enough video games based on it. For many reasons. First of all, the original broadcast last from [b]1966[/b] to [b]1969[/b]. And naturally, video games were barely there at that point (because yes, kids, there were times when video games didn't exist, believe it or not).

I mean, those were there, for quite some time too, but those were way too basic. For example, in [b]1966[/b] we've got games like [b]Frogmaster[/b] (some sort of mix between soccer and [b]Pong[/b] for mainframe computers with very basic visuals) and [b]Eliza[/b] (one of the earliest and most influential chatterbots in history). But it wasn't only that. See, [b]Star Trek[/b] ratings during the original [b]NBC[/b] broadcast were pretty low and the show even ended up being cancelled. Mostly because of the [b]NBC[/b] being a bunch of stupid a-holes who decided to move it to [b]10:00pm[/b] time slot, which was obviously a bad idea, but still, the original broadcast wasn't really that successful. Sure, the show got an army of dedicated fans (there were student-led protests, there were letter-writing campaigns and even [b]Isaac Asimov[/b] himself supported the show), but in the end, the show started to get real popularity only in [b]70s[/b], after entering television syndication. And that's where fun started.

We've got unlicensed games for personal computers, we've got dedicated systems (like [b]Star Trek: Phaser Battle[/b]), we've got some basic games like [b]Star Trek: Phaser Strike[/b] for [b]Microvision[/b] (later re-released without [b]Star Trek[/b] license as just [b]Phaser Strike[/b]) and so on. And when [b]Star Trek[/b] was resurrected as a major motion picture, following the success of [b]George Lucas[/b]' [b]Star Wars[/b]? We've got ourselves a pretty juicy vectors-based arcade called [b]Star Trek: Strategic Operations Simulator[/b], we've got [b]Star Trek: The Motion Picture[/b] for [b]Vectrex[/b] and finally, [b]Simon & Schuster Interactive[/b] joined the fun and released some awesome interactive fiction titles that I love with all of my heart. We also got a couple of arguable games like very confusing [b]Star Trek: The Rebel Universe[/b] and [b]Star Trek V: The Final Frontier[/b], which, despite some awesome artwork, I still consider to be the very worst [b]Star Trek[/b] game ever made, but unfortunately for all of the original series fans, that's where [b]The Next Generation[/b] show came in. And naturally, we started to get video games based on it. With [b]The Transinium Challenge[/b] for [b]Macintosh[/b] being the first of them (psst! Wanna buy some [b]Transinium[/b] from completely reliable [b]Ferengi[/b] trader?).

But guess what? [b]TOS[/b] wasn't done yet. Because right for its [b]25th Anniversary[/b], the show finally got video game adaptation it deserved. Well, a bit later actually. Since the original version of this game was released only in [b]1992[/b], while all we've got in [b]1991[/b] was that charming yet [i]extremely[/i] confusing thing for [b]NES[/b] (heck, I actually prefer the [b]Game Boy[/b] game over it), but still, here it is. The ultimate [b]Star Trek[/b] game.

As you can easily tell by looking at screenshots, it's an old-school point-and-click adventure. But it's not really that simple. What's cool about this game is that it captures the atmosphere perfectly. It isn't just a point-and-click adventure in [b]Star Trek[/b] setting. It [i]is[/i] [b]Star Trek[/b]. First of all, the game is divided into seven episodes and designed after the original TV show format. In other words, in this game you'll play through seven different episodes of your favorite show, with each episode being a separate story. There'll be mysteries, there'll be plot twists, there'll be [b]Klingons[/b] (who were among the biggest villains during the original series times) and so on. Playing this game? It's like living and breathing the original show. And it feels awesome.

And guess what? Gameplay is surprisingly advanced here too. For two reasons. First – our usual point-and-click gameplay became way deeper thanks to how we can use all of the tools from the show. See, among the other things, [b]Star Trek[/b] was a show about exploration. And this game? It actually rewards you for doing that. Make sure to use your [b]Starfleet[/b] and medical tricoders to scan everything. Not only you'll get more clues that way, you'll also get better score from your superiors. See, missions here are pretty non-linear and there's a way to actually fail them. Make sure to think about what you're doing. And yes, this game would even allow you to put phasers on stun. [i]How cool is that?![/i].

But there's also another thing about this game. And that thing is – space exploration. You'll control the [b]USS Enterprise[/b] and fly from one planet to another, while trying to avoid dangers. Talking about dangers, by the way. In this game? You'll be able to participate in space battles. And those are the most arguable part. I mean, [i]technically[/i] those are totally cool. You'll give orders to the crew, put the shields up (yes, you can't beam down with your shields up, the simulation is [i]that[/i] cool), select the warp speed, fire phasers and photon torpedoes, etc. Unfortunately, the space battles are also unpolished as heck. Seriously, the final battle (some battles here can't be avoided) here is, like, one of the most frustrating things I've ever experienced in video games. And I'm a pretty experienced player who played games like [b]Wing Commander[/b] before. Imagine point-and-click players who never played such stuff being forced through all that? It's kind of a disaster, really.

And yet, there's no way in the world to skip this game. Especially since what we have here is not the original floppy release. It's an [b]Enhanced CD-ROM Edition[/b] that comes with some extra cutscenes and, most importantly, the voiceover. I mean, we all love those enhanced [b]CD[/b] re-releases with voices (remember when [b]Kane[/b] himself, AKA [b]Joe Kucan[/b], voiced [b]Brandon[/b] in [b]The Legend of Kyrandia[/b]?), but this time? This time it's just special. Because, believe it or not, the game was voiced by the original cast. [b]William Shatner[/b], [b]Leonard Nimoy[/b] (yes, I'm writing this review at his birthday), [b]DeForest Kelley[/b], [b]James Doohan[/b], [b]George Takei[/b], [b]Nichelle Nichols[/b], [b]Walter Koenig[/b]... [i]they're all here![/i] And the words just can't describe how awesome it feels to have such a deep and complicated [b]Star Trek[/b] experience with the original cast reprising their roles.

Like I said, playing this game is like living and breathing the original TV show. You consider yourself to be a fan? You should stop with everything and play this game right now. Well, how to judge a game that's approaching its 30th birthday? By comparing it to other games of similar age and genre, maybe.

So, for the genre- Star Trek 25th Anniversary is mainly a point & click adventure game, with a few space fights mixed in. Contemporaries are then Monkey Island (1991), Simon the Sorcerer (1993) or Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis. In other words, ST25A was made in the middle of the "Golden Age of Graphic Adventures". Bad luck.

The space battles, then- they have to compete with the likes of Wing Commander 1 & 2 (1990 and 1991) or X-Wing (1993). Oh my.

I could compare those games against each other all day, but in short- ST25A does not stand a chance against its competitors. Graphically sound, but surpassed by other titles, mostly very easy puzzles with (sudden) dead ends, clunky controls (not even a main menu).

So, why do I recommend it? As a game, it's rather middle ground. BUT it does have that unique Star Trek feel to it- voices from the original cast and music and sounds from the TV show create a trekkish atmosphere that kept me coming back for more. Long enough that I started to suffer some form of brain desease and actually had some fun during those horrible ballte sequences.

This is absolutly a must-have for any old-school ST-fan!

Fans of graphic adventures, though... this is you final warning. Leave the neutral zone and set course elsewhere, or suffer the consequences ;-)

Time to make my first review of a Star Trek game, and the chosen one had to be ST 25th Anniversary.
I do recall seeing this game box in the shelf of a PC game shop back in the day when it was launched, it said, “requires CD-ROM”.
Ouch! I barely had money to buy my Sound Blaster 16 Value, how could I afford a CD-ROM drive to play this game? So, I had to let it pass…
Luckily these old games came back at GOG and now Steam, and I could finally put my hands on it, but is it worth it? Let’s find out!

The good:
- Let me start by saying that the characters are voiced by the actors from the original TV show, and only this already makes the game 8 out of 10, but there is more…
- This version of the game has all dialogs voice over
- Game is presented in chapters, so it feels like you are interacting with the adventures of the original series crew in a 4th season which was never produced to the TV, but now came up in a game format
- The game chapters have excellent plots, with good references to the TV show, even bringing back some side characters from the show (I won’t spoil who)
- Environmental designs for planet surface areas and inside ships are very well done and in line with the original ST TV show aesthetic
- Sound design is very good and follows exactly the style of the original ST series
- There are lots of dialogs to be explored between the Enterprise crew members, and along the chapters when interacting with other characters
- Bones and Spock still can’t get to an agreement at sometimes :D
- The Enterprise computer has an interesting library which allows you to type a subject, and the computer will give you some details about it
- The player has some freedom to solve the situations diplomatically, or letting your phaser speak for you, but off course you will be rated by Star Fleet on how well you handle your assignments
- You get to play with Kirk, Spock and McCoy, to make the best use of their abilities to solve the puzzles or challenges presented in the missions
- Puzzles are very well done, and hard to solve like any other game from this era
- Good gameplay time (about 7 hours), with good replay ability as one can try to solve the missions thru other means or improve the Star Fleet rating of the missions up to 100%
- The point and click adventure and inventory systems work well, not falling behind when compared to the Lucas Art’s point and click adventure classics such as Day of the Tentacle

The bad:
- The ship combat system is not that good, but it's not difficult to get the hang on how to control the Enterprise and make the best use of its weapons and Scott’s help
- Some puzzles can be quite hard, so players which are not used to these old games might have to look for a walkthrough in the internet when getting stuck at some point
- You need the star map, which is in the game manual, to know to which star system you got to jump for your next assignment, so get the manual from the game Steam page otherwise you will jump to the wrong system and get attacked
- Like most games of this era, there is no volume control for sound fx and music, it's either on of off, so the Enterprise bridge sounds can get anoying at times
- The old graphics might not appeal to everyone, although it runs under DOSBox and you can edit its configuration file inside the game folder to make the game less pixelized

The ugly:
- It feels like ages since we had a decent Star Trek game, what the heck happened?
- Where is Star Trek TNG A Final Unit? We need this game too!!!

Final verdict: If you are a fan of the original Star Trek TV show and like point and click adventure games, this one is a must to have at your library!
This is not only a great game, but it also captures the spirit of the original TV show in such a way which you will only be able to see again in its sequel “Star Trek Judgment Rites”.

Terrific point and click adventure game perfectly captures the essence of the original Star Trek. I am a big fan of the original Star Trek so I found it an absolute joy to play through Star Trek: 25th Anniversary.

You play as Captain Kirk as you lead the Enterprise on a series of missions across the galaxy. Expect to bump into familiar faces such as Romulans and Klingons as well as new ones. Parts of the game take place on the Enterprise as you have battles against enemy vessels. Other parts of the game have you beam down to a planet or on to another ship as part of a landing party. The way that the missions unfold reminded me a lot of the episodes of Star Trek. It's great to hear the voices of the original cast members including William Shatner, Leonard Nimoy and DeForest Kelley. Arguably, the game's biggest weakness is its graphics. They do look pretty terrible so this is not a great game to look at. Also, I feel that this is a game where you need the manual to help you. I sometimes had no idea what planet I was meant to visit as the game's map does not tell you the names of the planets, you have to look in the manual. Unfortunately, having a virtual manual means you cannot have both it and the game open at the same time. I'm not particularly great at point and click games so I did get stuck every now and then. Also, a minor complaint I have is that every time I start the game, I have to sit through thirty seconds of dialog before I can load my save game. Other point and click games of the era such as Indiana Jones And The Fate Of Atlantis do not have this problem.

Star Trek: 25th Anniversary does have some minor flaws but this is the ideal game for any Star Trek fan.

Star Trek 25th Anniversary to wydany oryginalnie w 1991 roku point & click z elementami kosmicznej strzelanki. Wcielając się w legendarnego kapitana Jamesa Tiberiusa Kirka stajemy przed 7 wyzwaniami, które są raczej luźno ze sobą powiązanie. Pozwolicie więc, że nie będę streszczał wszystkich "odcinków"? Tak, użyłem tego słowa bowiem, każda misja jest bardzo silnie stylizowana na typowy odcinek "The Original Series". Tytuł na tle pędzącego przez galaktykę Enterprise. Klimat oryginalnej serii aż kipi z ekranu. W czym pomagają oczywiście dźwięki znane z małego ekranu i zaangażowanie aktorów znanych z serialu. Robią niesamowitą robotę, po prostu nie mogę wyjść  podziwu jak moja rówieśniczka jest dopieszczona pod względem audio-wizualnym. Grafika to oczywiście pixel art i pseudo 3D w trakcie bitew kosmicznych, ale DOSBox (bo na nim odpala się ta wersja - przygotowana przez GOG tak swoją drogą) pozwala na wygładzenie krawędzi, więc jeśli komuś przeszkadzają piksele, gra dostarcza narzędzia pozwalające na poprawienie wrażeń na wyższych rozdzielczościach. Tak czy inaczej, pytanie brzmi, czy gameplay dotrzymuje kroku oprawie? Cóż. Tu bywa różnie. Gra jest napisana dość specyficznie. Zauroczyła mnie wierność telewizyjnemu oryginałowi, żeby przesłać się na planetę, najpierw musimy wlecieć na orbitę i wyłączyć osłony (te uniemożliwiają przesył, jeśli nie wiedzie), na powierzchni planety gra zaczyna przypominać typowego point & clicka, dość topornego (obsługa ekwipunku wymaga wprawy), ale przesympatycznego. Nie jest to jednak typowa przygodówka, w której gracz może sobie łazić w kółko i klikać co popadnie jeśli stracił rozpęd czy przeoczył linijkę dialogów. To znaczy, można, ale sporo się traci w ten sposób. Po pierwsze: punktację (na koniec misji dostajemy ocenę procentową), po drugie, fabułę. Wybierając dialogi - mamy tu opcje dialogowe, które wpływają na fabułę (i ocenę oczywiście) - jeśli nie są zgodne z charakterem postaci NPC reagują inaczej, niektóre sytuacje stają się trudniejsze i łatwiej jest umrzeć. Tak, to point & click, w którym umiera się całkiem często. Ta gra jest w 100% kierowana dla trekkies, którzy znają Kirka, Spocka czy McCoya lepiej niż własną rękę i doskonale wiedzą co by zrobili i co powiedzieli w konkretnych sytuacjach. Niestety, prawdopodobne przez nieuwagę twórców, można w ten sposób zablokować skrypty. Polecam częste sejwy, ale bez nadpisywania. Szczególnie w ostatniej misji, gdzie trzeba zrobić wszystko tak, jak zamyślili sobie twórcy, bo inaczej gra nie rozpocznie ostatniej sekwencji zagadek i Kirk, Spock i McCoy już na zawsze utkną w niedziałającym statku dryfującym w przestrzeni kosmicznej. Ah, nie wspomniałem o bitwach kosmicznych. Te również są niesamowicie wierne oryginałowi. By rozpocząć ostrzał trzeba poprosić Chekova by włączył uzbrojenie, w czasie gdy Scotty pilnuje by nic się nie rozleciało (warto mu zwracać uwagę na które elementy statku powinien mieć szczególną uwagę). Samo strzelanie jednak jest zwykłym celowniczkiem. obracamy się w kółko i walimy ze wszystkiego, co mamy w przeciwników. Daje to sporo satysfakcji, zwłaszcza, gdy otoczy nas dwóch lub więcej przeciwników, a my daliśmy im radę w tym "latającym muzeum", jak nazywa ją Scotty. 
Podsumowując. Jako trekkie i fan ponit & click, jestem zachwycony. Ta gra ma wszystko, piękną grafikę pixel art, akcję, wciągającą fabułę, naszych ukochanych bohaterów i ich oryginalne głosy, te cudowne dźwięki z lat 60, tę wspaniałą muzykę, no cudo. POLECAM. Jednakże. jeśli nie jesteś maniakiem klasycznych point & click, ciężko będzie ci docenić tę grę, jeszcze trudniej, jeśli nie zdążyłeś/aś zapoznać się z oryginalną serią Star Treka. Nie mówcie, że nie ostrzegałem.

Overall a really great game but the last mission was bugged for me.

There are two bugs that kept me from entering the final battle and made mme spent at least an hour and a half trying to get past these bugs. Slight spoilers ahead. The first one was where if Spock doesn't inspect the torpedo/weapons system then there's a chance you'll never be able to complete the game and wait for your death. The second bug was after getting everything ready for your surprise attack against the priates, and successfully blowing up the pirates, the game suddenly says the pirates boarded and it's game over. I had to replay the last part at least 10 times because I would randomly get a game over because the pirates board but yet they just been disabled. I just got lucky once and managed to get into the final battle sequence of the game.

Now the final battle is hard in this game. I would say the difficulity is surprising because up to the last point in the game you don't really have that much practice with battling with your enterprise ship. You might not be prepared for it and sometimes you have to get lucky. My tip to new players is that you should save, save, save! What I did was destroyed the first two pirate ships first, then I saved with the last remaining ship on there. Now the final ship (which I can't spoil but you'll know it's very unique) is very elusive. The trick I found is to go in reverse and try to go the opposite direction rather than following it on your radar. So basically you follow opposite, hit reverse, then you get a clear straight sight. Another trick is if your ship is badly damanged from the two pirate ships, you can heal/repair the ship by simply going really fast and constantly trying to actually "follow" the ship on radar rather than going in the opposite direction. Wait until you're fully repaired, then engage the target. Just remember to save at least once so that if you mess up you can reload and not have to destroy the other ships.


I enjoyed this game. I felt it was buggy in many parts and I'm not sure if it is due to it being on dosbox or what. A minor bug is you meet Harry Mudd but in one part of the game Mudd falls ill, but if you travel back to the first part of the mission you see him digging and sorting in the box, unaware of his counterpart. I didn't think it was a bug and instead thought it was similar to the Star Trek show where Mudd created all these androids and I was trying to foil his plans but I found out the makers of the game never intended for you to leave the fallen Mudd behind.

I recommend this game to all Star Trek fans. The final battle is a real surprise for me in terms of difficulity and I think it is worth it to see the ending. Just don't give up! It has a nice gesture to a very special person and a good thing to hear from William Shatner.
